t: Solve Two Sum in one pass with a hash map
desc: Given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target (exactly one solution, can't reuse an element). Do it in a single pass using a value-to-index hash map.
check: Your solution runs in O(n) time and O(n) space with a single scan
For each element you look up target minus it before inserting the current element
You correctly return indices (not values) and handle duplicates like [3,3], target 6

t: Detect a cycle in a linked list with Floyd's two pointers
desc: Given the head of a singly linked list, determine whether it contains a cycle. Use a slow pointer moving one step and a fast pointer moving two; they meet iff there is a cycle. Then extend it to find the cycle's start node.
check: Your detection uses O(1) extra space (no hash set of visited nodes)
You correctly return false for a null or single-node list with no cycle
Your extension finds the entry node of the cycle and you can justify why resetting one pointer to head works

t: Find the longest substring without repeating characters
desc: Given a string, find the length of the longest substring containing no repeated characters. Use a sliding window with a map of each character's last seen index, moving the left edge past any repeat as you scan right.
check: Your solution is O(n) with the window never moving left backward
For 'abcabcbb' you return 3 and for 'bbbbb' you return 1
You can explain how you jump the left pointer when a repeat's prior index is inside the window

t: Implement binary search and its lower-bound variant correctly
desc: Write binary search on a sorted array returning an exact match index, then write lower_bound: the first index whose value is >= a target. Pay careful attention to loop invariants and off-by-one in the boundary version.
check: Exact search returns the correct index or -1 and never infinite-loops
lower_bound returns the correct insertion point, including when the target exceeds all elements (returns n)
You can state your loop invariant and why your mid computation avoids overflow

t: Solve Merge Intervals by sorting on start
desc: Given a list of intervals [start,end], merge all overlapping intervals and return the non-overlapping set. Sort by start, then sweep, extending the current interval's end when the next start is within it, else emitting it.
check: Overlapping and touching intervals (e.g. [1,3],[2,6] -> [1,6]) merge correctly
Your solution is O(n log n) dominated by the sort
You handle fully contained intervals (e.g. [1,10],[2,3]) without splitting them

t: Validate a BST with recursive min/max bounds
desc: Given a binary tree, decide whether it is a valid binary search tree: every node's value is greater than all in its left subtree and less than all in its right. Recurse carrying an allowed (low, high) range for each node.
check: You reject a tree where a deep node violates an ancestor's bound (not just the parent)
Your solution handles duplicate values per your chosen strict/non-strict rule and edge integer limits
You can explain why checking only node-vs-children is insufficient

t: Compute level-order traversal of a binary tree with BFS
desc: Given the root of a binary tree, return its values grouped level by level, top to bottom, left to right. Use a queue and process one full level per outer iteration by capturing the queue size before draining it.
check: Output groups nodes by depth in the correct left-to-right order
You handle an empty tree (return empty) and a skewed tree correctly
You can explain how capturing the level size separates levels without a sentinel

t: Solve the 0/1 Knapsack with dynamic programming
desc: Given item weights and values and a capacity W, choose a subset maximizing value without exceeding W (each item used at most once). Build a DP over items x capacity, then optimize to a 1D array iterated right to left.
check: Your 2D DP returns the optimal value and you can reconstruct which items were chosen
Your 1D optimization iterates capacity in descending order and you explain why
You can state the time and space complexity in terms of n and W

t: Find number of islands with flood fill (DFS/BFS)
desc: Given a 2D grid of '1' (land) and '0' (water), count connected groups of land (4-directionally adjacent). Scan the grid; on each unvisited land cell, flood-fill its whole island (marking visited) and increment the count.
check: You count diagonally separate land as distinct islands (only 4-directional connectivity)
You avoid revisiting cells so the total work is O(rows*cols)
You handle all-water and all-land grids, and avoid stack overflow on a large grid (or note the risk)

t: Implement Dijkstra's shortest path with a min-heap
desc: Given a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights and a source, compute shortest distances to all nodes. Use a priority queue, popping the closest unfinalized node and relaxing its edges, skipping stale heap entries.
check: Distances are correct on a graph with multiple paths of differing weight
You skip outdated queue entries (lazy deletion) instead of using a decrease-key
You can explain why Dijkstra fails with negative edges and what to use instead

t: Compute the maximum subarray sum with Kadane's algorithm
desc: Given an integer array (possibly with negatives), find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum and return that sum. Track a running best-ending-here, resetting it when it would go negative, and a global maximum.
check: You return the correct sum for an all-negative array (the least-negative single element)
Your solution is a single O(n) pass with O(1) extra space
You can extend it to also report the start and end indices of the best subarray

t: Generate all subsets and all permutations via backtracking
desc: Given a set of distinct integers, produce (a) all subsets (the power set) and (b) all permutations, using recursive backtracking that chooses/unchooses each element. Ensure no duplicates when the input has none.
check: You generate exactly 2^n subsets and n! permutations for n distinct elements
Your recursion correctly undoes each choice (restores state) before trying the next
You can explain how to adapt the subset code to skip duplicate subsets when inputs repeat

t: Solve Trapping Rain Water with two pointers
desc: Given an array of non-negative bar heights (unit width), compute how much water is trapped after rain. Use two pointers moving inward, tracking left-max and right-max; the shorter side determines the water at each step.
check: You return the correct total for [0,1,0,2,1,0,1,3,2,1,2,1] (which is 6)
Your solution is O(n) time and O(1) space (no prefix-max arrays)
You can explain why the smaller of the two running maxima bounds the water at a position

t: Implement an LRU cache with a hash map plus doubly linked list
desc: Build a cache with get(key) and put(key,value) both in O(1), evicting the least recently used entry when capacity is exceeded. Use a hash map to nodes of a doubly linked list ordered by recency; move touched nodes to the front.
check: Both get and put run in O(1) and a get counts as a use (updates recency)
Exceeding capacity evicts exactly the least-recently-used key
You correctly update both the map and the list on eviction and on overwrite of an existing key

t: Solve Course Schedule with topological sort (cycle detection)
desc: Given numCourses and prerequisite pairs [a,b] meaning b must precede a, decide whether all courses can be finished (i.e. the directed graph is acyclic). Use Kahn's algorithm on in-degrees, or DFS with a visiting/visited coloring.
check: You return false exactly when the prerequisite graph contains a cycle
With Kahn's algorithm you can also output a valid ordering of courses
You can explain how the three-color DFS distinguishes a back edge from a cross/forward edge

t: Check balanced parentheses with a stack
desc: Given a string of brackets '()[]{}', determine if it is valid: every opener has a matching closer of the same type in the correct order. Push openers; on a closer, pop and check it matches, failing fast on mismatch or empty.
check: You reject '([)]' and accept '([]{})'
An unmatched leftover opener at the end returns false
A closer with an empty stack returns false immediately

t: Reason about Big-O: amortized, average, and worst case
desc: Work through why a dynamic array's push is amortized O(1), why hash map operations are average O(1) but worst O(n), and the difference between worst-case and average-case analysis, using concrete resizing/collision examples.
check: Why is appending to a dynamic array amortized O(1) despite occasional O(n) resizes?
When does a hash map degrade to O(n) per operation, and what mitigates it?
What is the difference between amortized and average-case complexity?
a: Doubling capacity makes the total cost of n appends O(n), so the per-append average is O(1); the rare copy's cost is spread over many cheap appends.
When many keys collide into one bucket (bad hash or adversarial input); good hashing, load-factor-triggered resizing, or treeifying buckets mitigate it.
Amortized averages cost over a sequence with a per-sequence guarantee; average-case averages over an input distribution and can still have bad inputs.

t: Understand when to reach for a hash map, heap, or BST
desc: Compare the operations and complexities of hash maps, binary heaps, and balanced BSTs, and reason about which data structure fits problems needing fast lookup, top-k/priority, or ordered range queries.
check: Why can't a hash map answer 'give me the smallest key' or a range query efficiently?
When is a heap the right choice over a sorted array or a BST?
What does a balanced BST offer that a hash map does not?
a: Hash maps scatter keys with no order, so min/max and range queries would require scanning all entries (O(n)).
When you repeatedly need the min/max (or top-k) with cheap inserts and don't need full ordering; heap gives O(log n) push/pop and O(1) peek.
Ordered operations: in-order traversal, predecessor/successor, and range queries, all in O(log n), which hashing can't do.

t: Recognize the core patterns behind most array/string problems
desc: Study the recurring templates: two pointers, sliding window, prefix sums, binary search on the answer, and monotonic stack, and learn to map a problem's constraints to the pattern that fits before coding.
check: What signals in a problem suggest a sliding window rather than brute force?
When does 'binary search on the answer' apply, and what must be true of the predicate?
What class of problems does a monotonic stack solve in O(n)?
a: A contiguous subarray/substring with a constraint that grows/shrinks monotonically (e.g. sum <= k, at most k distinct), letting you slide instead of re-scan.
When the answer lies in a range and feasibility is monotonic (if x works, all larger/smaller do), you binary-search x and test feasibility each step.
Next-greater/next-smaller element problems: maintaining a stack that stays sorted lets you resolve each element's answer in amortized O(1).

t: Understand dynamic programming: states, transitions, and memoization
desc: Learn to formulate a DP: define the state precisely, write the recurrence (transition), identify base cases, and choose top-down memoization vs bottom-up tabulation. Reason about why overlapping subproblems make DP pay off.
check: What two properties must a problem have for DP to apply?
How do you decide the dimensions and meaning of your DP state?
When is top-down memoization preferable to bottom-up tabulation, and vice versa?
a: Optimal substructure (optimal solution built from optimal subproblem solutions) and overlapping subproblems (the same subproblems recur).
The state must capture just enough that the subproblem is independent of how you reached it; each varying quantity in the recurrence becomes a dimension.
Top-down is easier to write and only computes reachable states; bottom-up avoids recursion overhead/stack limits and enables space optimization over the table.
